neighboring_unit_entries.title: Why direct natural Möbius approximants require regularization
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The naive natural Möbius partial sums have useful pointwise and restricted L1 behavior yet diverge in the ambient Hilbert space. Proposed subsequences and logarithmic mollification do not remove a general lower bound showing that any bounded-scale Beurling approximation can approach the target only slowly. Together these facts motivate changing the summation mechanism rather than merely enlarging a cutoff.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Zero-free half-planes control truncated reciprocal-zeta sums
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The quoted Balazard-Saias estimate converts nonvanishing of zeta in a half-plane into uniform control of truncated Möbius Dirichlet sums relative to the reciprocal zeta function in an interior strip. This is the bridge later used to dominate the transformed finite natural approximants under the Riemann hypothesis.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Fourier-Mellin isometry turns closure into transform-space domination
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: The proof changes representation from the original Hilbert space to an isometric Fourier-Mellin transform space. This is the structural move that makes analytic estimates usable as norm-convergence evidence.

In essence what has been done is to apply a summability method to the
old natural approximation. The convergence on special subsequences both
of n and of ǫ is also necessary and sufficient, and it is proposed here to study
this alongside with other summability methods for the natural approxima-
tion.
A final remark is in order. Note that we did not employ the dependence
on n in the Balazard-Saias Lemma 2.1. This dependence would seem to be
closely connected to the slowness of approximation to −χ indicated in (1.2).

The proof of Theorem 1.1 provides in turn a new proof, albeit of a stronger
theorem, of the Nyman-Beurling criterion which bypasses the deep and com-
plicated Hardy space techniques. One should extend it to the Lp case, that
is, to the condition that ζ(s) does not vanish in a half-plane ℜ(s) > 1/p. It
should be clear also that we have shown this special equivalence criterion to
be true:
Corollary 3.1. The Riemann hypothesis is equivalent to the H-convergence
of fǫ,n as n → ∞ for all sufficiently small ǫ > 0.
